# Surveys - Practice Test - Year 9

Attempt all questions and show your working. Suggested time: 30 to 35 minutes.

## Section A: Consolidating (Questions 1-4)

**Question 1**

A news website reports: "We surveyed 800 Australian adults about how often they cook dinner at home."

(a) What is the sample size?

(b) What is the population the website wants to describe?

**Question 2**

Is each of these a census or a sample?

(a) Every student at a school is asked whether they like the new uniform.

(b) 50 shoppers at a shopping centre are asked about parking.

(c) The national Census, which every household in Australia must fill in.

(d) TV ratings worked out from 5000 households that have a ratings box.

**Question 3**

Which of these survey questions is a leading question? Explain your choice.

Question A: "How many hours of sleep did you get last night?"

Question B: "Don't you agree that school should start later in the morning?"

**Question 4**

In a survey of 400 people, 260 said they had used a food delivery app in the past month.

What percentage of the people surveyed said this?

## Section B: Standard (Questions 5-16)

**Question 5**

A sports website ran an online poll: "Should junior sport stop keeping scores?" It received 12 000 votes and reported that 70% voted yes.

(a) How many votes were "yes"?

(b) Give two reasons why this result might not represent the views of all Australians.

(c) Suggest one way to collect data that would better represent all Australians.

**Question 6**

An advertisement for Brand X toothpaste says: "9 out of 10 dentists recommend Brand X!" In small print at the bottom it says: "Based on a survey of 20 dentists, funded by Brand X."

(a) How many of the dentists surveyed recommended Brand X?

(b) Describe two concerns about how this data was obtained.

**Question 7**

A website survey asks: "Given how dangerous e-scooters are, should they be banned from footpaths?"

(a) Explain why this is a leading question.

(b) Rewrite the question so that it is neutral.

**Question 8**

For each survey method, describe one problem that could make the results unrepresentative.

(a) A phone survey that only calls landline numbers between 10 am and 2 pm on weekdays.

(b) A survey about how people get to work, handed out only to people waiting at a train station.

(c) A survey about how often people exercise, handed out only at a gym.

**Question 9**

A local news website ran the headline "Support for new skate park doubles!" Last year, 15% of 200 people surveyed supported the skate park. This year, 30% of 40 people surveyed supported it.

(a) How many people supported the skate park in each survey?

(b) Explain why the headline could be misleading.

**Question 10**

A report gives the results of a survey of Year 9 students about how they usually travel to school.

| Method | Number of students |
|---|---|
| Car | 185 |
| Bus | 120 |
| Walk | 95 |
| Bike | 60 |
| Train | 40 |

(a) How many students were surveyed?

(b) What percentage of the students walk?

(c) What percentage travel by car?

(d) The report says "Most students travel to school by car." Is this statement correct? Explain.

**Question 11**

You read an online article that claims "Teenagers spend more time on gaming than on homework, a new survey shows." The article gives no other details.

List three questions you would ask about how the survey data was obtained before deciding whether to trust the claim.

**Question 12**

A council emailed a survey about a new library to 2400 residents. Only 360 residents replied.

(a) What was the response rate, as a percentage?

(b) Explain how a low response rate could make the results biased.

**Question 13**

A news site shows a column graph of a survey: 52% of people said "Yes" and 48% said "No". The vertical axis of the graph starts at 45% instead of 0%.

(a) On the graph, the "Yes" column rises $52 - 45 = 7$ units above the bottom of the axis. How many units does the "No" column rise? How many times taller does the "Yes" column look than the "No" column? Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

(b) How many times larger is 52% than 48%, correct to 2 decimal places?

(c) Explain why this graph is misleading.

**Question 14**

Primary data is collected by you. Secondary data was collected by someone else. Classify each source as primary or secondary.

(a) A survey you run with your class about favourite lunch foods.

(b) Population figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics website.

(c) A newspaper article reporting the results of an opinion poll.

(d) Heights you measure of the players in your basketball team.

**Question 15**

A streaming app reports: "68% of Australians watch shows on their phone." The data came from a survey of 2500 of the app's own users, completed inside the app.

(a) How many of the people surveyed said they watch shows on their phone?

(b) Explain why the claim about "Australians" is not justified by how the data was obtained.

**Question 16**

Two reports describe support for a new national park.

Report A: 1000 adults were chosen at random from across every state and territory and contacted by phone. 41% supported the park.

Report B: 25 000 people voted in an online poll on a radio station's website. 78% supported the park.

Which report gives the more reliable estimate of support among all adults? Explain your answer, referring to how the data was obtained.

## Section C: Advanced (Questions 17-20)

**Question 17**

A survey report says that 600 people were surveyed: 250 were aged under 30 and 350 were aged 30 or over. Of those under 30, 64% said they get most of their news from social media. Of those aged 30 or over, 40% said this.

(a) How many people in each age group said they get most of their news from social media?

(b) What percentage of all 600 people said this?

(c) A website used this survey for the headline "Most Australians now get their news from social media." Give two reasons why this headline is not supported.

**Question 18**

A school canteen manager wants to find out whether students would like a healthier menu. The school has students in Years 7 to 12.

(a) Describe how the manager could choose a sample of students that represents the whole school.

(b) Write one neutral question the manager could ask.

(c) Describe one source of bias the manager should avoid, and how to avoid it.

**Question 19**

A news website publishes the headline "Survey shows 3 in 4 parents want homework banned." The details at the bottom say: "Online survey of 480 parents who follow our social media page, run for two days after we published the article 'Is Homework Ruining Family Life?'"

(a) How many of the parents surveyed want homework banned?

(b) Identify three features of how the data was obtained that could bias the result.

(c) Write a more accurate headline for these results.

**Question 20**

A transport survey asked 1200 people whether they were satisfied with local public transport. Last year 45% were satisfied. This year a new group of 1200 people was asked the same question and 54% were satisfied.

(a) How many more people were satisfied this year than last year?

(b) By how many percentage points did satisfaction rise?

(c) By what percentage did the satisfaction rate rise?

(d) One report says satisfaction is "up 9%" and another says it is "up 20%". Explain how both reports got their numbers, and which wording is clearer.
answers_md:
# Surveys - Answer Key

**Question 1**

Answer: (a) $800$ (b) Australian adults

**Question 2**

Answer: (a) census (b) sample (c) census (d) sample

**Question 3**

Answer: Question B; it suggests the answer the asker wants ("don't you agree"), pushing people to say yes.

**Question 4**

Answer: $65\%$ ($\frac{260}{400} \times 100$)

**Question 5**

Answer: (a) $8400$ (b) Any two: only visitors to that website could vote (self-selected, not random); people with strong views are more likely to vote; people may vote more than once; visitors to a sports site may not be typical of all Australians. (c) Survey a random sample of Australians (for example, chosen at random from all states and age groups).

**Question 6**

Answer: (a) $18$ (b) Any two: the sample is very small (20 dentists); the survey was paid for by Brand X, so it may be biased; we do not know how the dentists were chosen or what exact question was asked (they may have recommended several brands).

**Question 7**

Answer: (a) It tells people e-scooters are dangerous before asking, pushing them towards answering yes. (b) For example: "Should e-scooters be allowed on footpaths? Yes / No / Unsure".

**Question 8**

Answer: (a) Misses people without landlines (often younger people) and people who work during those hours. (b) Over-represents people who use the train, so it overstates train use. (c) Over-represents people who exercise a lot, so it overstates exercise.

**Question 9**

Answer: (a) last year $30$ people, this year $12$ people (b) The second sample is very small (40 people), the actual number of supporters fell, and different people were surveyed, so the doubling of the percentage may be due to chance rather than a real change.

**Question 10**

Answer: (a) $500$ (b) $19\%$ (c) $37\%$ (d) No. Car is the most common method, but $37\%$ is less than half, so it is not "most" students.

**Question 11**

Answer: Any three, such as: How many people were surveyed? How were they chosen (random or self-selected)? Who were they (age, location)? What exact question was asked? Who ran or paid for the survey? When was it done?

**Question 12**

Answer: (a) $15\%$ ($\frac{360}{2400} \times 100$) (b) The people who reply may not be typical; for example, people with strong opinions (or who use the library most) are more likely to reply, so their views are over-represented.

**Question 13**

Answer: (a) $3$ units; about $2.3$ times ($7 \div 3$) (b) about $1.08$ times ($52 \div 48$) (c) Starting the axis at 45% exaggerates the difference, making a small gap of 4 percentage points look like Yes is more than twice No.

**Question 14**

Answer: (a) primary (b) secondary (c) secondary (d) primary

**Question 15**

Answer: (a) $1700$ (b) Only the app's own users were surveyed, and they already watch shows on the app, so they are not representative of all Australians; the sample was not chosen at random from the whole population.

**Question 16**

Answer: Report A. It used a random sample from across the country, so it is more representative. Report B is larger but its voters chose themselves and were radio station listeners, so it is likely biased.

**Question 17**

Answer: (a) under 30: $160$; 30 or over: $140$ (b) $50\%$ ($\frac{300}{600}$) (c) Any two: 50% is not "most" (it is exactly half); we do not know how the 600 people were chosen, so they may not represent Australians; the two age groups had very different results, so the overall figure depends on how many of each age group happened to be surveyed.

**Question 18**

Answer: (a) A stratified random sample: choose a set number of students at random from each year level (for example from the roll), in proportion to the size of each year level. (b) For example: "Would you like the canteen to offer more healthy options? Yes / No / Unsure". (c) For example: surveying only students who visit the canteen, or only one year level; avoid it by choosing at random from all students. (Accept other valid sources, such as leading wording.)

**Question 19**

Answer: (a) $360$ (b) Any three: online and self-selected; only followers of that page; run straight after a one-sided article on homework, which may have influenced answers or attracted parents who dislike homework; short two-day window; we do not know the exact question. (c) For example: "3 in 4 parents who answered our online poll want homework banned." (Accept any headline that makes clear the result comes from a self-selected online poll.)

**Question 20**

Answer: (a) $108$ ($648 - 540$) (b) $9$ percentage points (c) $20\%$ ($\frac{9}{45} \times 100$) (d) "Up 9%" is the change in percentage points ($54 - 45$); "up 20%" is the relative increase ($9 \div 45$). Saying "up 9 percentage points" is clearer, because "up 9%" could be read as a 9% increase.
check_notes: All counts and percentages recomputed in Python; census/sample, primary/secondary and every explanation re-read against the question wording.
